## Scenario 1: Fish Fecundity 

Over 60 species of rockfish (*Sebastes spp.*) reside off the coast of California, many of which are economically important to both recreational and commercial fisheries. Understanding the reproductive potential of an exploited stock is critical to assessing the health and status of a fishery. Yellowtail and Blackgill rockfish were randomly collected from specific sites along the coast of California, at times that corresponded with the period of annual rockfish egg development and larval release. Samples of eggs or larvae from the ovary were collected and used to estimate relative fecundity ($\Phi_{rel}$), the number of viable eggs or larvae per maternal somatic weight (larvae/g). Researchers also collected a standard measurement of length on fish, known as the fish fork length (mm), which is the length from the tip of the head to the fork in the tail, to see if increased size was associated with increased measures of fecundity in female rockfish. Data are found in the file `fecundity-bgyt.csv`. *Data based on Beyer et al. 2015 Envir. Biol. Fishes*

## Scenario 2: Patch Reef Species-Area Relationships    

Small patch reefs can harbor many reef fishes because most fishes have a drifting larval phase to randomly disperse over patchy habitats. The presence of patchy habitats allows larvae to disperse over and connect up meta-populations and meta-communities. Thus, small patch reefs may play an important role in sustaining overall meta-populations and -communities. The species-area relationship (SAR) is one of the most important tools for conservation biology and landscape ecology to understand large-scale dynamics such as these. We want to examine the relationship of damselfish (*Pomacentridae*) assemblages to the area of a reef. They randomly selected 84 small patch reefs (0.05 - 45.4 m^2^). For each patch reef, you calculate the surface area of the reef, and conduct a survey to determine the species richness (number of different damselfish species) found on the reef. The data are found in `species-area.csv`. **Data based on Hattori & Shibuno 2010 Ecol Res**
